title: Where does a tree make its first cut?
hook: Eight labelled dots, one cut. Which cut leaves the two groups least mixed?

knows: that a classifier sorts examples into labels
doesNotKnow: how a decision tree picks its first question
that a mix score such as Gini, weighted by group size, ranks candidate cuts

misconception: A tree asks whichever question comes to mind first, or the one that makes one group perfectly pure.
objective: The learner can compare candidate cuts by weighted Gini impurity and say that a tree keeps the cut whose groups come out most alike, even when another cut gives one perfectly pure group.

claims.text: The labels 0, 0, 1, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1 at x = 1 to 8 are a toy, labelled 'Toy labels' on the stage.
claims.source: Brief 44 in company/domains/briefs/ai.md; LABELS in Demo.tsx.

claims.text: Weighted Gini for the cuts: 2|3 0.21, 4|5 0.19 (the lowest of all seven cuts), 6|7 0.38; the others are 1|2 0.36, 3|4 0.37, 5|6 0.30.
At 4|5 the left group 0, 0, 1, 0 has one stray and the right group is all 1s; at 2|3 the left group is pure but the stray 0 at x = 4 sits in the right group of six, which counts for more.

Gini impurity of a group is 1 minus the sum of squared label shares (0 = one label only, 0.5 = half and half for two labels), and CART-style trees choose the split that most reduces size-weighted impurity.
claims.source: Breiman, Friedman, Olshen & Stone 1984, Classification and Regression Trees (Gini index). Placing cuts between neighbouring values is a convention.

recall.question: A tree can cut A, giving one perfectly pure group of 2 and a mixed group of 10, or cut B, giving two groups of 6 with one stray each. How does it decide?
options: Always A: a perfectly pure group is best
It compares the size-weighted mix (e.g. Gini) of both groups for each cut and keeps the lower
It takes whichever cut comes first
recall.why: A pure but tiny group can leave a big mixed one behind. The tree weighs each group's mix by its size and keeps the cut with the lowest total.
